question: Y71
answer:
LEGAL POSITION — HEALTH AND SAFETY AT WORK ETC. ACT 1974 (c. 37), s.2, AS IN FORCE ON 21 NOVEMBER 2026

This is a statement of the statutory position, not compliance advice for any particular employer or workplace.

1. ANSWER

(1) The employer's general duty to employees is in section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. In the Act's own words:

    "It shall be the duty of every employer to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all his employees."

Three features of that wording matter: the verb is "ensure" (an absolute or guaranteed-result duty, not a duty to take reasonable care); the objects are "health, safety and welfare" (welfare included, not merely prevention of injury); and the beneficiaries are "all his employees".

(2) The qualification that limits the duty is the phrase "so far as is reasonably practicable" in s.2(1) itself. It is not a separate section and it is not defined in the Act.

2. THE DUTY IN CONTEXT: s.2(2)–(5)

s.2(2) is not a further duty but a non-exhaustive gloss on s.2(1): "Without prejudice to the generality of an employer's duty under the preceding subsection, the matters to which that duty extends include in particular—" and then, each expressly subject to the same reasonable-practicability standard:

  (a) provision and maintenance of plant and systems of work that are, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe and without risks to health;
  (b) arrangements for ensuring, so far as is reasonably practicable, safety and absence of risks to health in connection with the use, handling, storage and transport of articles and substances;
  (c) provision of such information, instruction, training and supervision as is necessary to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety at work of his employees;
  (d) so far as is reasonably practicable as regards any place of work under the employer's control, maintenance of it in a condition that is safe and without risks to health, and provision and maintenance of safe means of access and egress;
  (e) provision and maintenance of a working environment for his employees that is, so far as is reasonably practicable, safe, without risks to health, and adequate as regards facilities and arrangements for their welfare at work.

s.2(3) adds a distinct, non-SFAIRP-qualified duty: except in prescribed cases, every employer must prepare and as often as appropriate revise a written statement of general health and safety policy and the organisation and arrangements for carrying it out, and bring it (and any revision) to the notice of all employees.

s.2(4) is a regulation-making power: the Secretary of State may provide for recognised trade unions to appoint safety representatives from among the employees, who represent employees in consultations with the employer "under subsection (6)" and have such other functions as may be prescribed. (Subsection (6), the consultation duty, was not within the text extracted for this answer and is therefore referred to only as s.2(4) refers to it, not quoted.)

s.2(5) is repealed (shown in the current text as "F1(5). . . .").

3. WHAT THE QUALIFICATION MEANS

"Reasonably practicable" is not defined in the 1974 Act. Its content is judicial. The settled formulation is that of Asquith LJ in Edwards v National Coal Board [1949] 1 KB 704 (approved in Marshall v Gotham Co Ltd [1954] AC 300): a precaution is required unless the quantum of risk is insignificant in relation to the sacrifice (in money, time or trouble) needed to avert it; if the risk is significant and the sacrifice is not grossly disproportionate to it, the precaution must be taken. The standard is therefore not negligence's "reasonable care", and it is not a simple cost-benefit balance: cost only excuses non-compliance where it is grossly disproportionate to the risk. Foreseeability of the risk is a precondition of the duty biting at all.

Burden of proof: on a prosecution under s.33 for breach of s.2(1), the prosecution must first prove that employees were exposed to a risk to health or safety; the employer then bears the burden of showing that it was not reasonably practicable to do more (R v Chargot Ltd [2008] UKHL 73).

4. FURTHER LIMITS ON THE s.2(1) DUTY (distinct from the SFAIRP qualification, listed so the answer is not mistaken for an unqualified absolute duty)

  - Persons protected: s.2 protects "employees" only. Duties owed to persons other than employees (visitors, contractors, the public) arise under s.3, not s.2; duties relating to premises under s.4; to articles/substances for use at work under s.6; employees' own duties are in s.7.
  - Civil actionability: by virtue of s.47(2) HSWA as amended by s.69 of the Enterprise and Regulatory Reform Act 2013, breach of a duty in s.2 is not actionable in civil proceedings except in respect of regulations made under s.15 (most of which preserve civil liability). Criminal enforcement under s.33 is unaffected. The duty remains a criminal one.
  - Territorial extent: s.2 is marked "U.K." for extent on the statute book. For Northern Ireland workplaces, the operative general-duties regime is in substance replicated by the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978 (S.R. 1978/1039 (N.I. 9)); extent should be confirmed before relying on s.2 for a Northern Ireland workplace. Scotland and Wales are within the Act's application; health and safety is not a devolved matter in the relevant sense.
  - Prescribed exceptions apply to s.2(3) (written policy statement) only; there is no prescribed exception to s.2(1).

5. VERSION CONTROL FOR THE DATE "AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21"

Text relied on: legislation.gov.uk, Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, s.2, point-in-time version 16/07/2026 (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1974/37/section/2/2026-07-16), corroborated by the whole-Act point-in-time version of the same date (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1974/37/body/2026-07-16) and by the earlier snapshots of 31/01/2017 and 28/06/2022.

Why that snapshot answers the 2026-11-21 question:
  (a) The snapshot's own status line states the provision is "up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026" (whole-Act page: "on or before 23 November 2026"). 21 November 2026 falls inside that window.
  (b) The timeline of amendments for the Act lists amendment dates running to 14/10/2024, 27/01/2026 and 16/07/2026, with none between 16/07/2026 and 21/11/2026. There is therefore no intervening amendment to displace the snapshot.
  (c) The text of s.2(1) is word-for-word identical in the 06/04/2011, 31/01/2017, 28/06/2022 and 16/07/2026 snapshots. The general duty and its SFAIRP qualification have not been amended since enactment in 1974; the amendments to s.2 over time concern other subsections (and the repeal of s.2(5)). The answer is therefore insensitive to the choice of snapshot within that range.
  (d) Residual verification note: the page warns that "there are changes that may be brought into force at a future date". Such uncommenced amendments do not affect the text in force on 21/11/2026 unless commenced on or before that date, and the site's "in force on or before 22/23 November 2026" statement is the site's own assertion that commenced changes up to that date are reflected. If a belt-and-braces check is wanted, re-open https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1974/37/section/2 with the "What Version" selector set to 21/11/2026 and confirm the s.2(1) wording is unchanged; on the evidence above it will be.

6. CITATION FORM

Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (c. 37), s.2(1): duty of every employer to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare at work of all his employees; qualification: "so far as is reasonably practicable" in the same subsection, interpreted per Edwards v National Coal Board [1949] 1 KB 704 and Marshall v Gotham Co Ltd [1954] AC 300; burden per R v Chargot Ltd [2008] UKHL 73.

7. OUT OF SCOPE

This states the statutory position as at 21/11/2026. It is not an assessment of whether any particular employer has complied with s.2(1), does not address the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 or other subordinate instruments, and is not legal advice.

The first reads: "Act 1974, Section 2 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 22 November 2026."

question: Y72
answer:
ANSWER

1. The written statement (ask 2). Under s.2(3) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (c. 37) ('HSWA 1974'), every employer must prepare, and as often as may be appropriate revise, 'a written statement of his general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of his employees and the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy'. Two elements are therefore mandatory and must both appear in the document: (a) the general policy on health and safety at work of the employer's employees; and (b) the organisation and arrangements currently in force for carrying out that policy. The duty is a continuing one — 'prepare and as often as may be appropriate revise' — and the Act sets no fixed review period (there is no statutory annual review in s.2(3)); revision is triggered by appropriateness, i.e. by material change in the undertaking, its organisation or its arrangements.

2. The prescribed exceptions (ask 3). Section 2(3) opens with 'Except in such cases as may be prescribed'. The relevant prescription is the Employers' Health and Safety Policy Statements (Exception) Regulations 1975 (S.I. 1975/1584), made under the power in s.2(3) itself. Regulation 2 provides: 'Any employer who carries on an undertaking in which for the time being he employs less than five employees is hereby excepted as respects that undertaking from the provisions of subsection (3) of section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974'. Three points of construction matter: (i) the threshold is fewer than five employees in the undertaking — an employer with five or more employees in the undertaking has no exception; (ii) the exception is undertaking-specific ('as respects that undertaking'), so an employer with several undertakings may be excepted for one and bound for another; (iii) the exception is from the whole of s.2(3), i.e. from the duties to prepare, to revise and to bring to notice, not merely from the notice duty. The Act also contemplates that s.2(3) may be modified in particular sectors by other instruments (the annotations to s.2 record modifications of s.2(3) by, among others, S.I. 1993/1897 art. 4(4) and S.I. 2014/1663 reg. 4(2)); where such a modification applies to the undertaking it displaces or varies the s.2(3) position and must be checked for that sector.

3. To whom the statement and any revision must be brought (ask 4). Section 2(3) requires the employer 'to bring the statement and any revision of it to the notice of all of his employees'. The recipients are therefore all of the employer's employees — not a subset, not merely management, not merely safety representatives. The statutory verb is 'bring ... to the notice of', not 'provide copies to'; s.2(3) imposes a notice/publicity duty, not an express duty to issue a copy to each employee. Compliance is measured by effective communication to the whole workforce (for example by issuing the statement to every employee, by displaying it where all employees can readily see it, by electronic publication to all employees where that is accessible to all of them, or by a combination), and a method that leaves a class of employees (shift workers, remote or peripatetic workers, part-time or temporary staff) unaware of the statement will not discharge the duty. Separate and additional duties exist elsewhere — s.2(2)(c) (information, instruction, training and supervision), s.2(4)–(7) and the Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1977 (S.I. 1977/500) (safety representatives, consultation, safety committees; the annotations record that S.I. 1977/500 reg. 8(1) modifies s.2(4)) — but those do not enlarge or alter the class of persons to whom s.2(3) requires the statement and its revisions to be brought.

STATUTORY TEXT RELIED ON (s.2(3), HSWA 1974, verbatim)

'2 General duties of employers to their employees.
...
(3) Except in such cases as may be prescribed, it shall be the duty of every employer to prepare and as often as may be appropriate revise a written statement of his general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of his employees and the organisation and arrangements for the time being in force for carrying out that policy, and to bring the statement and any revision of it to the notice of all of his employees.'

VERIFICATION AGAINST THE 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21' CONSTRAINT (ask 1)

- The text of s.2(3) is identical in the as-enacted version and in the point-in-time versions at 1 October 2014, 1 October 2015 and 28 June 2022, as published on legislation.gov.uk. No amendment to s.2(3) is recorded in any of those versions; the recorded textual amendments to s.2 are the repeal of s.2(5) and a substitution in s.2(7) by the Employment Protection Act 1975, neither of which touches s.2(3).
- The point-in-time page for s.2 states that the provision 'is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 23 November 2026'. Because 21 November 2026 precedes 23 November 2026, that statement covers the target date, and it confirms that no change affecting s.2(3) is in force at 2026-11-21. The page also notes that there are changes that may be brought into force at a future date; those are prospective and do not affect the position at 2026-11-21.
- Extent: the Act's principal extent is Great Britain (England, Wales and Scotland); Northern Ireland has its own parallel provision in the Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978. Any answer for a Northern Ireland undertaking must be taken from that Order, not from s.2(3) HSWA 1974. Where the Act is applied outside Great Britain by order (e.g. S.I. 2001/2127, as amended), s.2 applies as so applied.
- Caveat on the exception instrument: S.I. 1975/1584 was checked in its as-made form, in which reg. 2 is quoted above. Before relying on the exception in a contentious matter, confirm the current version of S.I. 1975/1584 as at 2026-11-21 on legislation.gov.uk; the operative effect (undertakings with fewer than five employees excepted from s.2(3)) is the effect the Act contemplates and is stated in the instrument's own explanatory note, but a point-in-time confirmation of the instrument is the correct evidential step.

COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE AN ENGINEER OR SAFETY MANAGER CAN APPLY DIRECTLY

Step 1 — Determine whether the exception applies. Count the employees employed in the undertaking at the relevant time. If fewer than five, reg. 2 of S.I. 1975/1584 excepts that undertaking from s.2(3); record the basis of the determination (undertaking identified, headcount, date). If five or more, proceed. Re-test whenever headcount changes, because the exception is 'for the time being'.

Step 2 — Prepare the written statement with both mandatory components:
  (a) General policy: a statement of the employer's general policy with respect to the health and safety at work of his employees (commitment to so far as reasonably practicable ensuring health, safety and welfare; the aims and objectives; who owns the policy; the date of issue and signature of the most senior person in the undertaking).
  (b) Organisation and arrangements in force for carrying out that policy: named responsibilities at each level; competent persons and competent advice; arrangements for risk assessment and for implementing protective and preventive measures; arrangements for information, instruction, training and supervision (s.2(2)(c)); arrangements for consultation with employees and safety representatives and, where required, the safety committee (s.2(6)–(7)); arrangements for accident and incident reporting, first aid, emergency procedures and evacuation; arrangements for monitoring, audit and review; arrangements for co-operation with other employers sharing a workplace.

Step 3 — Establish the revision regime. The Act requires revision 'as often as may be appropriate'. Set triggers rather than a bare calendar: on any material change to the undertaking, plant, substances, processes, premises, organisation or workforce; on introduction of new legislation or approved codes of practice; on the findings of an accident investigation or enforcement action; and a periodic review (annual review is good practice, not a statutory requirement under s.2(3)). Record each revision, its date, and what changed.

Step 4 — Bring the statement and any revision to the notice of all employees. Design a method that demonstrably reaches every employee, including shift, part-time, temporary, remote and peripatetic workers: issue a copy (electronic or paper) to each employee and obtain an acknowledgement; display it in each workplace where all employees can readily see it; publish it on the internal system to which all employees have access. Document the method and the date, and record how each category of employee was reached. Because s.2(3) speaks of bringing to notice rather than of supplying copies, an acknowledgement-plus-display-plus-publication combination is the safest evidence of discharge.

Step 5 — Keep the evidence. Retain: the current statement (dated and signed); the revision history; the headcount determination supporting any reliance on reg. 2 of S.I. 1975/1584; and the distribution/notice records.

SCOPE NOTE

This is a statement of the position under s.2(3) HSWA 1974 and the exception prescribed by S.I. 1975/1584 reg. 2 as verified above. It does not address sector-specific modifications of s.2(3) by other instruments, the separate information and consultation duties owed to safety representatives, or the parallel Northern Ireland provision, each of which must be checked separately for the undertaking in question.

question: Y73
shape: UK health and safety arrangements recording threshold
answer:
DELIVERABLE — Legal-text lookup: Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (S.I. 1999/3242)

ANSWERS
- Ask 2 — Coming-into-force date: 29 December 1999 (page wording: "Coming into force 29th December 1999").
- Ask 3 — Employee-count threshold for recording the regulation 5(1) arrangements: 5 employees, i.e. "five or more employees". The duty bites at five; it is not "more than five".
- Ask 1 — Version used: the "Latest Available (Revised)" text (latest amendment listed in the Alternative versions timeline: 25/11/2021), not the "Original: King's Printer Version" and not any earlier amendment snapshot.

VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT (as fetched)
1) Instrument front matter — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242 :
   "Statutory Instruments / 1999 No. 3242 / HEALTH AND SAFETY / The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 / Made 3rd December 1999 / Laid before Parliament 8th December 1999 / Coming into force 29th December 1999"
2) Regulation 5, current/revised text — https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242/regulation/5 :
   "Health and safety arrangements E+W+S
    5.—(1) Every employer shall make and give effect to such arrangements as are appropriate, having regard to the nature of his activities and the size of his undertaking, for the effective planning, organisation, control, monitoring and review of the preventive and protective measures.
    (2) Where the employer employs five or more employees, he shall record the arrangements referred to in paragraph (1)."

VERSION SELECTION (Ask 1) — how the correct text was identified
- The page's own legend defines the options: "Latest Available (revised): The latest available updated version of the legislation incorporating changes made by subsequent legislation and applied by our editorial team"; "Original (As Enacted or Made): The original version of the legislation as it stood when it was enacted or made." The ask specifies the former, so the Original King's Printer version is excluded.
- The "Alternative versions" list on the reg 5 page runs 29/12/1999, 27/10/2003, 06/04/2006, 01/10/2006, 06/04/2007, 01/10/2011, 01/10/2013, 01/06/2015, 01/10/2015, 22/08/2020, 09/11/2020, 20/12/2020, 20/01/2021, 29/03/2021, 17/05/2021, 20/06/2021, 21/06/2021, 07/08/2021, 25/11/2021 — so the latest revised text is the 25/11/2021 state.
- The same page records: "There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, Section 5" (and the whole-instrument page records the same for the instrument). So on the supplied page, the revised text of reg 5 is the operative and complete version; no unapplied change is pending against reg 5.
- Version-insensitivity check on the threshold: the identical reg 5(1)–(2) wording appears in the 01/10/2015 snapshot (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242/2015-10-01/data.xht) as in the current text, so the "five or more" threshold is stable across the revised versions and is not an artefact of which snapshot was read.

READING NOTES / TRAPS GUARDED AGAINST
- Bound direction: the trigger is "five or more" (>= 5), so the threshold figure is 5. Reporting "more than 5" or "6" would contradict the quoted words and is expressly not what is stated here.
- Distinction preserved: reg 5(1) is the duty to make and give effect to arrangements (no employee-number qualifier); the recording duty is a separate obligation in reg 5(2) keyed to headcount. The answer to Ask 3 is the reg 5(2) recording threshold, not a condition on reg 5(1).
- Which date: 29 December 1999 is the instrument's coming-into-force date from the front matter. The dates in the "Alternative versions" / timeline list (e.g. 25/11/2021) are amendment/version dates and are NOT coming-into-force dates of the Regulations; they must not be substituted.
- Single commencement: the front matter gives one coming-into-force date for the instrument; no separate commencement order date is shown on the supplied page.
- Standard caveat on the source itself: the page states "Revised legislation carried on this site may not be fully up to date", but pairs this with "no known outstanding effects" for reg 5, so the quoted text is the best available statement on the supplied page.

REPRODUCTION / VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (so a reviewer can confirm both values independently)
1. Open https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242 ; confirm the version selector is on "Latest Available (Revised)"; read the front matter lines "Made / Laid before Parliament / Coming into force" — record 29th December 1999.
2. Open https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3242/regulation/5 ; confirm the version selector is on the latest revised state (post-25/11/2021); read reg 5(2) — record "five or more employees".
3. Cross-check the version list at the foot of the reg 5 page: the last entry (25/11/2021) must be the selected version; if a later amendment appears, re-read reg 5(2) from that later text before restating the threshold.

SAFETY-OFFICER COMMENT (scope)
This is a text-extraction task, not a compliance determination. Practical consequence for duty-holders, stated only as far as the quoted text supports: at five or more employees the employer must record the reg 5(1) arrangements; below five, reg 5(2) imposes no recording duty (other recording obligations elsewhere in the Regulations or in other instruments are outside the scope of this answer and must be checked against their own provisions on the page). question: Y74
answer:
ANSWER FOR THE COMPLIANCE FILE

Question: Under the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (SI 1999/3242), as in force on 21 November 2026, do the Regulations apply to the master or crew of a ship, or to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master?

Answer: NO. The Regulations are expressly disapplied in those circumstances by regulation 2(1). The disapplication covers all three categories of person named in the question — the master, the crew, and the employer of the master or crew — and it is not limited to the master and crew alone.

Scope clause relied on: SI 1999/3242 reg. 2(1) (regulation 2, headed 'Disapplication of these Regulations'), with the definitions in reg. 2(3). Extent: E+W+S.

1. THE PROVISION, VERBATIM

Regulation 2 (as substituted by S.I. 2003/2457, reg. 3, with effect from 27 October 2003) reads, so far as material:

  '2.—(1) These Regulations shall not apply to or in relation to the master or crew of a ship, or to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew which are carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master.

   (2) Regulations 3(4), (5), 10(2) and 19 shall not apply to occasional work or short-term work involving work regarded as not being harmful, damaging or dangerous to young people in a family undertaking.

   (3) In this regulation—
   "normal ship-board activities" include—
     (a) the construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship outside, but not inside, Great Britain; and
     (b) the repair of a ship save repair when carried out in dry dock;
   "ship" includes every description of vessel used in navigation, other than a ship belonging to Her Majesty which forms part of Her Majesty's Navy.'

Paragraph (2) is a separate disapplication (young persons in a family undertaking) and is not engaged by this question. Paragraph (3) supplies the two definitions that govern paragraph (1).

2. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT ANALYSIS OF REG. 2(1)

The disapplication operates only if every one of the following is satisfied. Each is a separate condition, and the answer changes if any one of them fails.

(a) The person must be 'the master or crew of a ship, or ... the employer of such persons'. All three are named. The employer of the master or crew is expressly within the disapplication, not merely the individuals on board. The wording is 'to or in relation to', which is broad: it reaches the employer's obligations in relation to those persons, not only obligations owed to them on board.

(b) The subject-matter must be 'the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew'. The definition in reg. 2(3) is inclusive ('include'), not exhaustive, so the two listed items are illustrations, not a closed list: (i) the construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship outside, but not inside, Great Britain; and (ii) the repair of a ship, except repair carried out in dry dock.

(c) Those activities must be 'carried out solely by the crew'. If persons who are not crew participate in the activity, the 'solely' condition is not met on the ordinary meaning of the words, and the disapplication cannot be relied on for that activity.

(d) The activities must be 'under the direction of the master'. If the crew are acting under the direction of someone else for the activity in question, the condition fails.

(e) 'Ship' is defined in reg. 2(3) as including 'every description of vessel used in navigation', but expressly excluding a ship belonging to Her Majesty which forms part of Her Majesty's Navy. The disapplication therefore does not extend to Royal Navy ships.

3. WHAT THE ANSWER DOES AND DOES NOT COVER — THE BOUNDARIES

Because reg. 2(1) is activity-specific and condition-specific, the following fall OUTSIDE the disapplication, and the Regulations therefore continue to apply to them (subject to the separate question of territorial application at paragraph 5):

- Activities that are not 'normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew' — for example, the shore-side management of the undertaking, the employment of shore-based staff, and crew training or other work carried out ashore.
- Activities not carried out 'solely by the crew' — for example, where a shore-based technician, contractor or other non-crew person takes part in the activity.
- Activities not carried out 'under the direction of the master'.
- Repair of a ship carried out in dry dock. This is expressly carved back in by the words 'save repair when carried out in dry dock' in reg. 2(3)(b): dry-dock repair is not within 'normal ship-board activities', so the disapplication does not reach it.
- Construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship carried out inside Great Britain. Reg. 2(3)(a) covers such work only when done 'outside, but not inside, Great Britain'; the same work done inside Great Britain is not within 'normal ship-board activities'.
- Any ship belonging to Her Majesty which forms part of Her Majesty's Navy (excluded from the definition of 'ship').

A single employer or a single individual may therefore be inside the Regulations for some activities and outside them for others on the same day. The correct unit of analysis is the activity, not the person or the vessel.

4. WHAT THE DISAPPLICATION DOES NOT MEAN

Reg. 2(1) disapplies the 1999 Regulations only. It does not of itself remove any other duty. In particular, the general duties in the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (including the provisions applied to ships by section 84 and by the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (Application outside Great Britain) Order 2013) and the merchant shipping health and safety regime administered by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency are separate regimes and are outside the scope of this answer. A negative answer under reg. 2(1) should not be recorded in the compliance file as 'no health and safety duties apply'; it should be recorded as 'the 1999 Regulations do not apply; parallel regimes to be assessed separately'.

5. TERRITORIAL POINT (FLAGGED, NOT ANSWERED)

Reg. 2(1) is expressed without a territorial limitation of its own, while the instrument's extent is E+W+S. Whether a particular ship, voyage or offshore installation is within the reach of the Regulations at all is a question under the 1974 Act and the Application outside Great Britain Order, and is not resolved by reg. 2(1). That question is outside the four corners of this answer and should be recorded as a separate open item if the ship operates outside Great Britain.

6. 'AS IN FORCE ON 21 NOVEMBER 2026' — BASIS AND RESIDUAL RISK

- Reg. 2 was substituted in its current form with effect from 27 October 2003 by S.I. 2003/2457, reg. 3 (recorded as textual amendment F1/F3 on the legislation.gov.uk versions).
- The text of reg. 2 is identical in the point-in-time versions at 20 June 2021, 25 November 2021 and 3 April 2023; no textual amendment to reg. 2 after 27 October 2003 is recorded.
- The 3 April 2023 revised version records 'There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999', and the instrument's change timeline lists no amendment later than 25 November 2021.
- On that evidence the provision in force on 21 November 2026 is the provision quoted at paragraph 1 above.
- Residual risk to be closed before the file is signed off: legislation.gov.uk is a revised database and is not certified as current to the day. Before filing, re-open the 'latest available (revised)' version of SI 1999/3242 regulation 2 and confirm (i) no amendment to reg. 2 after 3 April 2023, and (ii) the 'Changes to Legislation' note remains 'no known outstanding effects'. If any amendment is found, re-run this analysis against the amended text; the structure of the answer (three cumulative conditions, three categories of person) would survive, but the wording would need to be re-quoted.

7. FORM OF WORDS FOR THE COMPLIANCE RECORD

'Regulation 2(1) of the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (S.I. 1999/3242), as in force on 21 November 2026, provides that the Regulations "shall not apply to or in relation to the master or crew of a ship, or to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew which are carried out solely by the crew under the direction of the master". Accordingly, the Regulations do not apply to the master, the crew, or the employer of the master or crew in respect of normal ship-board activities of the ship's crew carried out solely by the crew under the master's direction. This disapplication is confined to activities meeting all of those conditions; it does not extend to activities that are not normal ship-board activities, that are not carried out solely by the crew, that are not under the direction of the master, to repair carried out in dry dock, to construction, reconstruction or conversion of a ship inside Great Britain, or to a ship belonging to Her Majesty forming part of Her Majesty's Navy. Parallel duties under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and the merchant shipping health and safety regime are outside the scope of this note and are assessed separately.'

8. AUTHORITY

Text quoted from the official legislation database, legislation.gov.uk, SI 1999/3242: regulation 2 point-in-time views at 20/06/2021, 25/11/2021 and 03/04/2023, and the whole-instrument plain-extent view. The result is consistent with the Halsbury's Laws commentary (vol. 52 (2020), para. 393), which states that the 1999 Regulations 'do not apply to or in relation to the master or crew of a ship, or to the employer of such persons, in respect of the normal ship-board activities of a ship's crew'.

question: Y75
shape: UK power press thorough examination intervals
answer:
THOROUGH EXAMINATION OF POWER PRESSES — PUWER 1998, PART IV, REGULATION 32(4)

1. ANSWER AT A GLANCE

| Case | Maximum interval between thorough examinations |
|---|---|
| Power press with fixed guards only | At least every 12 months |
| Any other case (guards other than fixed guards only, and/or protection devices — e.g. interlocked movable guards, light curtains, two-hand controls) | At least every 6 months |
| Additional event | Each time that exceptional circumstances have occurred which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the power press or its guards or protection devices |

In every case the power press itself is examined, and its guards and protection devices are examined while in position on that power press (reg 32(4)(a)). These are maximum intervals: examination at least that often, and sooner whenever the third trigger fires.

2. INSTRUMENT AND VERSION (asks 1 and 2)

Instrument: The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, SI 1998/2306, Part IV (Power Presses), regulation 32 — 'Thorough examination of power presses, guards and protection devices'. Reg 32 in force 5.12.1998 (reg 1).

Version: The revised text on the supplied page (legislation.gov.uk, Part IV, E+W+S, with the 'Changes to Legislation' note and 'there are currently no known outstanding effects for … PART IV' statement; regulation 32 data.xml carries the Statute Law Database metadata and expert participation dated 2018-07-30) reproduces reg 32(4) in the same words as the original as-made version and the 1999-11-29 point-in-time version. There is therefore no version divergence on these intervals or on the additional trigger; the answer below is the revised-version text.

3. THE STATUTORY TEXT RELIED ON (reg 32(4), revised version, quoted)

"(4) For the purpose of ensuring that health and safety conditions are maintained, and that any deterioration can be detected and remedied in good time, every employer shall ensure that—
(a) every power press is thoroughly examined, and its guards and protection devices are thoroughly examined when in position on that power press—
(i) at least every 12 months, where it has fixed guards only; or
(ii) at least every 6 months, in other cases; and
(iii) each time that exceptional circumstances have occurred which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the power press or its guards or protection devices; and
(b) any defect is remedied before the power press is used again."

Supporting definitions in the same regulation: reg 32(7) — "'defect' means a defect notified under regulation 34 other than a defect which has not yet become a danger to persons."

4. HOW TO CLASSIFY THE PRESS (the 'fixed guards only' test)

- 'Fixed guards only' means the press is safeguarded solely by guards that are fixed (they can be removed only with the use of a tool) and there is no protection device and no movable/interlocked guard in the safeguarding arrangement. That case attracts the 12-month interval.
- 'Other cases' means any safeguarding arrangement that is not fixed guards only — a movable or interlocked guard, a photoelectric presence-sensing device, a two-hand control, a hold-to-run control used as a protective measure, or any combination of these with fixed guards. That case attracts the 6-month interval.
- The classification is a property of the press as safeguarded at the time of examination, not a permanent label. If a press is converted from fixed-guards-only to interlocked guarding (or the reverse), the interval changes with it; the change should be recorded in the examination schedule at the point of conversion.
- Two scope conditions must be checked before applying either interval:
  (a) Reg 31: regulations 32 to 35 do not apply to a power press of a kind described in Schedule 2. Confirm the press is not a Schedule 2 excluded press before scheduling examinations.
  (b) Reg 32(6): paragraph (4) does not apply to that part of a closed tool which acts as a fixed guard. Such a tool-mounted fixed guard is instead examined under reg 32(3) before it is used on a power press. So a press whose only safeguarding is a closed-tool fixed guard is not thereby automatically on the 12-month cycle for that element; the press is still examined under 32(4) and the closed-tool guard element is handled under 32(3).

5. THE ADDITIONAL EVENT (reg 32(4)(a)(iii))

Beyond the periodic cycle, a thorough examination is required each time that exceptional circumstances have occurred which are liable to jeopardise the safety of the power press or its guards or protection devices. The regulation states the trigger; it does not list the events. As a safety engineer, the events I would define as exceptional circumstances in the employer's examination schedule — and treat as triggering an immediate examination before further use — include: an incident or near miss involving the press or its safeguarding; impact or collision damage (e.g. a die crash, press jam cleared under load, forklift strike); a defect notified under reg 34; unauthorised modification or defeat of a guard or protection device; major repair, re-build or replacement of a clutch, brake, drive or control system; a guard or protection device that has been altered or disturbed other than in the course of tool adjustment; structural cracking or fatigue indications; and fire, flood or other damage to the press or its safeguarding. These are illustrative engineering examples of the statutory trigger, not statutory wording.
- Consequence of the trigger firing: examine, then remedy any defect before the press is used again (reg 32(4)(b)).

6. RELATED TRIGGERS THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER TO ASK 5 (do not conflate)

- Reg 32(1): a power press must not be put into service for the first time after installation, or after assembly at a new site or in a new location, unless thoroughly examined (installed correctly and safe to operate) and any defect remedied. This is a one-off commissioning examination, not a periodic interval.
- Reg 32(2): a guard (other than a closed-tool fixed guard) or protection device must not be put into service for the first time on a power press unless thoroughly examined in position on that press and any defect remedied.
- Reg 32(3): that part of a closed tool acting as a fixed guard must not be used unless thoroughly examined in position on any power press in the premises and any defect remedied.
- Reg 33: this is inspection and testing of guards and protection devices — after setting, re-setting or adjustment of tools, and before use beyond the fourth hour of a working period — by a competent appointed person who signs a certificate. Inspection under reg 33 is not thorough examination under reg 32 and does not discharge the 12-month/6-month cycle.
- Reg 32(5): transitional rule — where a press, guard or protection device was already subject to thorough examination under reg 5(2) of the Power Presses Regulations 1965, the first examination under reg 32(4) was due before the date the 1965 requirement would have fallen due. Historical only.

7. PROCEDURE TO PUT THIS INTO EFFECT

Step 1 — Inventory. List every power press; for each, record whether it falls within Schedule 2 (reg 31 exclusion).
Step 2 — Classify. For each in-scope press, record the safeguarding arrangement and assign the interval: fixed guards only = 12 months; anything else = 6 months. Record the basis for the classification and the date of the last thorough examination.
Step 3 — Schedule. Set the next due date as last examination date + 12 months or + 6 months respectively (never later). Do not extend an interval because a press has been idle; the trigger for the next examination is the elapse of the interval or the occurrence of exceptional circumstances, whichever is sooner.
Step 4 — Competence and appointment. Appoint a competent person to carry out the thorough examination; that person must be able to detect deterioration and judge whether the press, its guards and its protection devices remain safe to operate. Under reg 34 the examiner must notify the employer forthwith of any defect which in the examiner's opinion is or could become a danger to persons, and report on the examination.
Step 5 — Event trigger. Define in writing, in the examination schedule, the events the employer treats as exceptional circumstances (section 5 above), and require that any such event stops the press until a thorough examination has been carried out and any defect remedied.
Step 6 — Defect control. No re-use until every defect is remedied (reg 32(4)(b)); link this to the permit-to-work/lock-off procedure so a press cannot be restarted while an examination finding is open.
Step 7 — Records. Retain the examination reports and the schedule showing the classification and due dates, so the interval applied to each press is auditable. (The specific content and retention requirements of regs 34 and 35 are not reproduced in the supplied passages; take those from the instrument itself and from HSE's approved code of practice L112, Safe use of power presses, ISBN 9780717666201, published 12-12-2014, rather than from this note.)
Step 8 — Review. Re-classify on any change of guarding, tooling or location, and re-set the due date accordingly.

8. LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

This answer states the statutory thorough-examination intervals and the additional statutory trigger under PUWER 1998 reg 32(4) as shown in the revised version on the supplied page. It does not address: whether a particular press is excluded by Schedule 2; the reg 34/35 report content and retention detail; the reg 33 inspection regime in full; or any additional examination interval imposed by other legislation or by an employer's own higher standard. Where an employer's risk assessment or the L112 approved code of practice sets a shorter interval, the shorter interval governs in practice.

question: Y76
answer:
# Legal advice: does PUWER 1998 apply to a distributor in respect of equipment supplied by sale?

**Date of advice / law stated as at:** 21 November 2026
**Jurisdiction:** Great Britain (England and Wales, Scotland). PUWER 1998 is a GB instrument (extent E+W+S). Northern Ireland is governed by the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1999 (SR 1999/279) — this advice does not cover NI.

---

## 1. Answer

**No.** The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998, as in force on 21 November 2026, do **not** apply to a distributor in respect of work equipment that it supplies by way of sale. The scope clause is **regulation 3**, and the operative disapplication is **regulation 3(5)**, which is in these terms:

> "(5) The requirements imposed by these Regulations shall not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by him by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement."

That wording is confirmed in three independent sources fetched for this advice: the revised text of the whole instrument, the revised text of regulation 3 (extent view), and HSE's L22 Approved Code of Practice and guidance.

---

## 2. Version of the text in force on 21 November 2026

- The legislation.gov.uk 'Changes over time' view for regulation 3 lists only two versions: **05/12/1998 (as made)** and **01/10/2015 (amendment)**.
- The instrument contents page records: "There are currently no known outstanding effects for The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998", and regulation 3 likewise shows no outstanding effects.
- The fetch was made on 23 November 2026, i.e. *after* the operative date, and the revised text carried no later amendments. The text in force on 21 November 2026 is therefore the **01/10/2015 version**.
- The only 2015 change material to regulation 3 is the substitution in **3(3)(a)** of "[relevant self-employed person]" for "self-employed person" (consequent on the Deregulation Act 2015 / Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 (General Duties of Self-Employed Persons) (Prescribed Undertakings) Regulations 2015). **Regulation 3(5) was not amended.**
- Caution for anyone citing HSE L22: the L22 PDF in the source set prints the *pre-2015* wording ("to a self-employed person, in respect of work equipment he uses at work"). L22 is reliable for the wording of 3(4) and 3(5), which are unchanged, but the revised legislation.gov.uk text governs where they differ.
- **Evidential gap flagged, not filled:** the fetched passages of regulation 3 begin at paragraph (2). **Regulation 3(1)** was not captured and is therefore not quoted in this advice. It is not needed for the answer, because the operative rule for a seller is 3(5), which is verified verbatim. Anyone relying on this note for a purpose that turns on 3(1) should read it from the revised text first.

---

## 3. The scope clause in full (regulation 3, as in force 21 November 2026)

Verified verbatim (paragraphs (2)–(5)):

> "(2) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer in respect of work equipment shall apply to such equipment provided for use or used by an employee of his at work.
>
> (3) The requirements imposed by these Regulations on an employer shall also apply—
> (a) to a [relevant self-employed person], in respect of work equipment he uses at work;
> (b) subject to paragraph (5), to a person who has control to any extent of—
>   (i) work equipment;
>   (ii) a person at work who uses or supervises or manages the use of work equipment; or
>   (iii) the way in which work equipment is used at work,
> and to the extent of his control.
>
> (4) Any reference in paragraph (3)(b) to a person having control is a reference to a person having control in connection with the carrying on by him of a trade, business or other undertaking (whether for profit or not).
>
> (5) The requirements imposed by these Regulations shall not apply to a person in respect of work equipment supplied by him by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement."

Paragraphs (6)–(10) (verified in part) are the merchant-shipping carve-outs: subject to (7)–(10), the Regulations impose no obligation in relation to a ship's work equipment, whether used on or off the ship; (7)–(8) deal with shore employers relying on merchant shipping requirements; (9) preserves regulations 7–9, 11–13, 20–22 and 30 for ship's work equipment used in a specified operation; (10) deals with activities specified in the 1995 Order. These do not bear on a seller of ordinary work equipment and are noted only for completeness of the scope clause.

Related definitions (regulation 2(1)) — **not reproduced in the verified extracts**, so confirm against the revised text before relying on them: "work equipment" is defined in the familiar terms *any machinery, appliance, apparatus, tool or installation for use at work (whether exclusively or not)*; and "employer", except in regulation 3(2) and (3), "includes a person to whom the requirements imposed by these Regulations apply by virtue of regulation 3(3)(a) and (b)" (this last point **is** verified, from L22).

---

## 4. Analysis

**4.1 Who the scope clause binds.** Regulation 3 imposes PUWER's requirements on three categories only: (i) employers, in respect of work equipment provided for use or used by their employees at work (3(2)); (ii) relevant self-employed persons, in respect of equipment they use at work (3(3)(a)); and (iii) persons having control, to the extent of that control, where the control is held in connection with the carrying on of a trade, business or other undertaking (3(3)(b) read with 3(4)). A distributor selling goods is none of these *in respect of that supply*.

**4.2 The express supplier carve-out.** Regulation 3(5) is not a mere omission; it is a positive disapplication. Even if a seller could be characterised as a person "having control to any extent" of the equipment (for example because it specifies, configures or commissions it), 3(3)(b) is expressly made "subject to paragraph (5)", and 3(5) removes the requirements entirely "in respect of work equipment supplied by him by way of sale, agreement for sale or hire-purchase agreement". For the sale transaction itself, the answer is therefore a clean **no**.

**4.3 Scope of the carve-out — limits the client must know.**

| Supply route | Within reg 3(5)? | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Outright sale | Yes ("by way of sale") | PUWER requirements do not apply to the seller in respect of that equipment |
| Agreement for sale (e.g. conditional sale, sale with retention of title pending payment) | Yes | Same |
| Hire-purchase | Yes (expressly named) | Same |
| **Hire / leasing / rental** | **No — not named** | The seller-turned-hirer gets no protection from 3(5) and may be a person "having control" under 3(3)(b) (e.g. where it retains maintenance, inspection, servicing or instruction duties), to the extent of that control |
| Private sale by an individual | Outside reg 3 in any event | Not an employer, relevant self-employed person or trade/business controller in respect of the supply |

This is a reading of the words of 3(5) (hire and leasing are conspicuously absent from a list that expressly names hire-purchase), not a quotation from guidance. Treat it as analysis and, where a client both sells and hires, do not assume 3(5) covers the hire book.

**4.4 Own use by the distributor.** The carve-out is directed at the supply. Where the same business also *uses* the equipment at work as an employer (demonstrations, testing, showroom use by employees, loan of plant to its own sites), it may be subject to PUWER in that separate capacity under 3(2), and it should not assume 3(5) is a blanket immunity across all capacities. The literal width of "in respect of work equipment supplied by him" creates genuine ambiguity here; the purposive reading (3(5) exists because the *supply* transaction is regulated by product-safety law, not by use-based duties) is to confine it to the supply capacity. Practical consequence: a distributor who also uses the goods at work should comply with PUWER for that use and not rely on 3(5).

**4.5 Regulation 10 is not a supplier duty.** Regulation 10 (conformity with essential requirements) is addressed to "every employer" and does not impose obligations on a seller as such. It is not a route to attaching PUWER to the distributor.

**4.6 What still applies to the distributor (PUWER's exclusion is narrow).** Being outside PUWER for the sale does not leave the distributor unregulated:
- **Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, section 6** — duties on persons who design, manufacture, import or supply articles for use at work: to ensure so far as reasonably practicable that the article is designed and constructed to be safe and without risks to health when properly used; to carry out or arrange necessary testing and examination; and to make available adequate information about the use for which it is designed and tested and the conditions necessary for safe use. This is the principal duty that bites on a seller.
- **Product-supply legislation**, e.g. the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 (as amended) and the Electrical Equipment (Safety) Regulations 2016, including marking, technical-file and importer obligations where the distributor is also the importer.
- **HSWA sections 2 and 3** in respect of its own employees and its own undertaking.

---

## 5. Practical checklist for the distributor

1. **Confirm capacity.** Is the transaction a sale, an agreement for sale, or hire-purchase (within 3(5)) — or hire/leasing (outside it)? Paper the answer; the hire book is the exposure.
2. **Confirm the goods are "work equipment"** within regulation 2(1) (machinery, appliance, apparatus, tool or installation for use at work). Note that even if they are, 3(5) still disapplies PUWER for the sale.
3. **Confirm no own-use.** If the business uses the equipment at work (demos, trials, hire fleet), apply PUWER to that use rather than relying on 3(5).
4. **Do not treat 3(5) as the compliance answer.** The operative regime for the supply is HSWA s.6 plus the applicable product-supply regulations; PUWER's exclusion is a scope rule, not a defence to a product-safety failure.
5. **Check jurisdiction.** GB only. For NI, apply SR 1999/279 (equivalent provision, separately verified).
6. **Cite properly.** Quote regulation 3(5) verbatim and cite "PUWER 1998, reg 3(5), as in force 21 November 2026". Do not cite L22's text of 3(3)(a), which pre-dates the 2015 substitution.

---

## 6. Sources relied on

- The Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/2306), revised text, whole instrument — reg 3(2)–(5) quoted verbatim (fetched 2026-11-23).
- SI 1998/2306, regulation 3, extent view — reg 3(2)–(10) quoted verbatim; version history showing 05/12/1998 and 01/10/2015 only, and "no known outstanding effects" (fetched 2026-11-23).
- SI 1998/2306, contents (England) — confirms no outstanding effects for the instrument (fetched 2026-11-23).
- HSE, *Safe use of work equipment* (L22), ACOP and guidance — reg 3(2)–(6) quoted verbatim; reg 2(1) definition of "employer" quoted (fetched 2026-11-23). Note: L22 prints the pre-2015 wording of reg 3(3)(a).
- HSE, *PUWER 1998* guidance — reg 3(2)–(6) quoted verbatim, corroborating the same wording.

**Caveat on completeness:** regulation 3(1) and the regulation 2(1) definition of "work equipment" were not present in the verified extracts and are flagged as unverified above; neither affects the answer, which turns on regulation 3(5).

question: Y77
answer:
SAFETY ENGINEER'S DETERMINATION — COSHH 2002, reg 9(4): retention of LEV examination/test and repair records

ANSWER (ask 2): At least 5 years, running from the date on which the record was made.

=====================================================================
1. THE GOVERNING PROVISION AND ITS TEXT
=====================================================================
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations 2002 (SI 2002/2677), regulation 9 (Maintenance, examination and testing of control measures), paragraph (4):

  "(4) Every employer shall keep a suitable record of the examinations and tests carried out in accordance with paragraphs (2) and (3) and of repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests, and that record or a suitable summary thereof shall be kept available for at least 5 years from the date on which it was made."

Regulation 9(2)(a) is the LEV examination-and-test duty that feeds this record: thorough examination and testing of local exhaust ventilation plant at least once every 14 months, or at the shorter interval in Column 2 of Schedule 4 for plant used with a Schedule 4 process. Regulation 9(3) covers thorough examination/testing of non-disposable RPE. Both paragraphs (2) and (3) are captured by the paragraph (4) record duty.

So the record duty is: LEV examinations and tests + repairs carried out as a result of those examinations and tests -> record kept available >= 5 years from the date the record was made. A suitable summary may stand in place of the full record, and carries the same 5-year retention.

=====================================================================
2. WHAT THE "5 YEARS" ATTACHES TO, AND FROM WHEN
=====================================================================
- The clock starts on "the date on which [the record] was made" — i.e. the date the examination/test record (or repair record) was created, which in practice is the examination date or the date the examiner's report is received and entered.
- It does NOT run from "the date of the last entry made in it". That formulation belongs to regulation 10(5) (exposure monitoring records). Do not import it into regulation 9(4).
- Each record carries its own 5-year clock. A site with 14-monthly LEV examinations will therefore hold, at any moment, roughly the last 4-5 examination records plus any intervening repair records.
- The obligation is "at least" 5 years — a floor, not a target. Longer retention is lawful and may be prudent (occupational disease latency, civil claims, insurance, RPE/LEV modifications that later become relevant to an exposure investigation).
- "Available" means retrievable and producible on request; regulation 9(4) imposes no fixed location and no cessation-of-trade notification duty (contrast regulation 10(7)(c) and regulation 11(4)(c), which do require notification to the Executive and transfer of monitoring/health records when the employer ceases to trade — those duties do not extend to regulation 9 records). Access is reinforced by other routes: HSE inspectors' powers to require production of records under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 s.20, and safety representatives' rights under the Safety Representatives and Safety Committees Regulations 1977 / the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 reg 7. Treat the record as needing to be producible within the timescale an inspector or an employee representative would reasonably expect, including for LEV serving a process operated by a contractor.

=====================================================================
3. THE 40-YEAR TRAP — DO NOT CONFUSE THESE FOUR DIFFERENT CLOCKS
=====================================================================
The single most common error in answering this question is quoting 40 years. 40 years applies to exposure-monitoring records and health records, not to regulation 9 LEV records.

  Record type | Provision | Minimum retention | Clock starts
  LEV / engineering control examination & test records, and repairs resulting | reg 9(4) | 5 years | date the record was made
  RPE thorough examination/test records | reg 9(4) (via reg 9(3)) | 5 years | date the record was made
  Exposure monitoring records representative of identifiable employees' personal exposure | reg 10(5)(a) | 40 years | date of the last entry made in it
  Other exposure monitoring records (e.g. fixed-site/static) | reg 10(5)(b) | 5 years | date of the last entry made in it
  Health records (health surveillance) | reg 11(3) | 40 years | date of the last entry made in it

Note also that the 14-month (or Schedule 4) figure in reg 9(2)(a) is an examination FREQUENCY, not a retention period. It does not modify the 5-year retention in any way.

=====================================================================
4. "RECORD OR A SUITABLE SUMMARY" — WHAT THAT PERMITS
=====================================================================
The employer may keep either the full record or a suitable summary. Two points of construction:

(a) "Suitable" is not defined. As a matter of safe practice a summary is suitable only if it preserves what the full record would be relied on for: identification of the LEV plant (and the process it serves), date of the thorough examination and test, the examiner (name and competence basis), the results/findings (including any defect, its severity and the control/containment performance outcome), the repairs carried out as a result, the date of those repairs, and the next examination due date. A summary that records only "LEV examined — satisfactory" is not defensible: it cannot evidence that repairs were done or that a defect was closed out.
(b) The 5 years runs "from the date on which it [the record] was made". The summary stands in the place of the record, so the summary must be kept available for at least 5 years from the date the underlying record was made — not 5 years from the date the summary itself was created. The conservative and compliant rule is therefore: hold the summary on the same clock as the record it replaces. If the full record is later destroyed while the summary is relied on, the summary inherits the remainder of the 5-year period, not a fresh one.

Guidance content for a thorough examination and test record (not law, but the benchmark an inspector will apply) is in HSE HSG258, Controlling airborne contaminants at work, and the COSHH Approved Code of Practice L5.

=====================================================================
5. WORKED RETENTION DATES (apply directly to a retention schedule)
=====================================================================
Rule: earliest permissible destruction date = (date the record was made) + 5 years + 1 day. Retaining to the end of the calendar year following the 5-year anniversary is a simple, always-compliant administrative rule.

  Record made (LEV exam/test or repair) | 5 years elapses | May be destroyed no earlier than
  2026-11-21 | 2031-11-21 | 2031-11-22
  2027-03-15 | 2032-03-15 | 2032-03-16
  2028-01-31 | 2033-01-31 | 2033-02-01
  2029-07-01 | 2034-07-01 | 2034-07-02

For a 14-monthly examination regime, a compliant register will typically hold 4-5 live examination records plus any repair records at any point in time.

=====================================================================
6. IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE (what a site should actually do)
=====================================================================
Step 1 — Register. Maintain a single LEV register listing every item of LEV plant (ID, location, process served, Schedule 4 process flag, examination interval, next due date).
Step 2 — Record at the point of examination. For every thorough examination and test, capture: plant ID; date of examination/test; examiner name and competence/ accreditation; methods and results (including static pressure, transport velocity or equivalent performance measures where used); defects and their risk rating; date the record was made; next examination due date.
Step 3 — Record repairs as a distinct linked entry. For each repair carried out as a result of an examination/test, record: linked examination record ID, defect, repair description, date completed, who did it, and post-repair verification. Regulation 9(4) requires the repairs themselves to be recorded, not merely the fact that a defect was found.
Step 4 — Set the retention field. On creation, stamp the record with retention = date made + 5 years; automated systems should set a disposal-eligible date of date made + 5 years + 1 day and block earlier deletion.
Step 5 — Summary path. If the full examiner's report is not retained (e.g. it is held by the contractor), obtain and retain a suitable summary meeting the paragraph 4(a) content list, stamped with the same retention date as the underlying record.
Step 6 — Availability. Keep records retrievable for the site, for the employees and their representatives who work with the LEV, and for inspectors; include contractor-operated LEV serving the site's processes within the same register.
Step 7 — Disposal. At the disposal-eligible date, dispose unless a hold applies (live claim, investigation, enforcement action, occupational-disease enquiry). Log the disposal.

=====================================================================
7. VERSION / CURRENCY POSITION AS AT 2026-11-21
=====================================================================
The wording of regulation 9(4) quoted above is identical in the original (as made, in force 2002-10-24), the point-in-time version at 2002-11-21, the consolidated version at 2007-07-01, and the consolidated version at 2008-12-01, and is reproduced unchanged in the current HSE COSHH Approved Code of Practice L5. No amendment to regulation 9(4) is identified in any of the material examined, and none of the amendments made to COSHH 2002 since 2002 touches the regulation 9 record-retention period.
Residual verification item (does not change the answer, but should be closed before the determination is relied on for enforcement-facing work): a point-in-time consolidated view of SI 2002/2677 specifically at 2026-11-21 was not retrieved; the answer rests on the identity of the regulation 9(4) text across four point-in-time versions spanning 2002-2008 plus the current ACOP. If a pre-publication check is required, confirm on legislation.gov.uk that the 'latest available (revised)' version of regulation 9(4) carries no amendment annotation before 2026-11-21.

=====================================================================
8. SCOPE OF THIS DETERMINATION
=====================================================================
This answers only the retention question for regulation 9 examination/test and repair records (including RPE records captured by reg 9(3)-(4)). It does not address: the adequacy or frequency of the thorough examination and test itself (reg 9(2), Schedule 4); the content standard for a 'thorough examination and test' under HSG258; exposure-monitoring or health-record retention (regs 10 and 11); or records required by other regimes (e.g. LOLER, PUWER, DSEAR) that may apply to the same plant in parallel.

## Answer

The responsible person must send the report **as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident** — i.e. no later than the 15th calendar day after the date of the accident, counting the day after the accident as day 1.

- Outside limit: **15 days**.
- Event from which it runs: **the date of the accident** (not the end of the seven-day incapacity period).
- Days: calendar days, not working days; weekends and bank holidays are not excluded.

## Statutory basis (as in force on 2026-11-21)

Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 2013, S.I. 2013/1471, **regulation 4(2)**:

> "Where any person at work is incapacitated for routine work for more than seven consecutive days (excluding the day of the accident) because of an injury resulting from an accident arising out of or in connection with that work, the responsible person must send a report to the relevant enforcing authority in an approved manner as soon as practicable and in any event within 15 days of the accident."

Regulation 4(3) provides that regulation 4 is subject to regulations 14 and 15; those carve-outs qualify *whether/who* must report in specified cases and do not alter the 15-day period for this category.

**Version check performed.** The point-in-time text retrieved from legislation.gov.uk carries page-version metadata of 2026-04-08 (Expert Participation 2026-04-06) and records no known outstanding effects amending the over-seven-day provision; the wording of regulation 4(2) is therefore the wording in force on 2026-11-21. Caveat to note on file: the pages were retrieved on 2026-11-23, 48 hours after the target date, so the check is "no amendment identified between 2026-04-08 and retrieval"; if a hard audit trail is needed, re-pull the point-in-time version dated 2026-11-21 from legislation.gov.uk and attach it to the report file.

## How the 15 days are counted

1. Take the **date of the accident** (day 0).
2. The next day is day 1; the deadline is the end of **day 15** (date of accident + 15 calendar days).
3. The seven-day incapacity test runs on the same convention: the day of the accident is excluded, so day 1 of incapacity is the day after the accident and the "more than seven consecutive days" threshold is crossed when incapacity extends into **day 8**.

**Worked example (accident Monday 2 March 2026):**

| Item | Date |
|---|---|
| Accident (day 0, excluded) | Mon 2 Mar 2026 |
| Incapacity day 1 | Tue 3 Mar 2026 |
| Incapacity day 7 | Mon 9 Mar 2026 |
| Threshold exceeded — duty crystallises | Tue 10 Mar 2026 (day 8) |
| Reporting deadline (day 15) | **Tue 17 Mar 2026** |

Practical window: 10–17 March inclusive = 8 days. Note the compression — the clock runs from the accident, so by the time you can know the seven-day test is met you have already used 8 of the 15 days. Report on day 8, not on day 15.

If you prefer a belt-and-braces margin against any argument that the accident day itself counts as day 1 (which would advance the deadline by one day), file by the earlier of the two dates. The regulation's own primary duty — "as soon as practicable" — makes early filing the compliant course in any event.

## What must be sent, and by whom

- **Responsible person**: for an employee, the employer; otherwise the person in control of the premises/undertaking in which the person at work was working (reg. 2).
- **Means**: "in an approved manner" — in practice the HSE online report form (or the equivalent approved route for the relevant enforcing authority, e.g. ORR for railways). Keep the submission reference.
- **Recipient**: the relevant enforcing authority (HSE or the local authority, depending on the activity).
- **Content**: the particulars required by Part 2 of Schedule 1 (including the injured person's details, date/time/place, a brief description of the circumstances, and the injury).

## Related duties that are often confused with this one

- **Over-three-day record** (reg. 12(1)(b)): an injury incapacitating for more than three consecutive days (accident day excluded) must be **recorded** — not reported — and the record kept at least 3 years. The over-seven-day *report* is additional to this.
- **Specified injuries** (reg. 4(1) and the reporting procedure in Part 1 of Schedule 1): notify the enforcing authority by the quickest practicable means without delay, then send a report in an approved manner within 10 days of the event. A case can be both a specified injury and an over-seven-day injury; both duties then apply.
- **Fatality within one year of a reported injury** (reg. 6(3)): notify without delay, whether or not the injury was already reported.
- **Dangerous occurrences, occupational diseases, carcinogen/biological-agent exposures** (regs 7–9): separate triggers and routes; the 15-day figure is specific to reg. 4(2).

## Compliance procedure for the responsible person

1. Record the accident date, time and place on the day it happens; open an incident file.
2. Diarise incapacity days from the day after the accident; confirm the >7-consecutive-day test on day 8 (calendar days, consecutive — a return to work followed by fresh absence does not necessarily break consecutiveness; treat the sequence conservatively).
3. On the day the test is met (day 8 at the latest), submit the report in the approved manner and record the submission reference, date and time.
4. Hard stop: do not allow submission to slip past **date of accident + 15 calendar days**, irrespective of weekends or leave.
5. Keep the reg. 12 record (over-three-day entry) and the report submission evidence for at least 3 years.

## Limits of this answer

This is a statement of the legal position and a compliance procedure, not legal advice on a specific incident; where the case is complex (self-employed person, non-employee at work, multi-employer premises, Crown/armed-forces exemptions under regs 14–15), take advice from the enforcing authority or a solicitor. Breach of the reporting duty is an offence under section 33 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974.

ANSWER — 49 CFR Part 213 (Track Safety Standards), § 213.53(a), as in force on 2026-11-21, U.S. standard-gauge track

Governing text (verbatim, § 213.53(a), "Gage"):

  "(a) Gage is measured between the heads of the rails at right-angles to the rails in a plane five-eighths of an inch below the top of the rail head."

1. WHERE BETWEEN THE RAIL HEADS (ask 3)

Gage is measured between the HEADS of the two rails — that is, from the gage-side (inner, flangeway-facing) face of one rail head to the gage-side face of the opposite rail head — taken AT RIGHT ANGLES to the rails. It is not measured between rail centerlines, between web or base locations, or along the rail's longitudinal axis. The measurement is the clear transverse distance between the two heads at the specified elevation; it is a width (a distance across the track), not a depth.

Note on the gloss: the regulation says "between the heads of the rails"; identifying those surfaces as the gage-side faces of the heads is the standard field interpretation of the phrase and is consistent with the regulation's own usage elsewhere (e.g., § 213.55 footnotes refer to points "on the gage side of the line rail ... below the top of the railhead"). The quoted words, not the gloss, are the controlling text.

2. HOW FAR BELOW THE TOP OF THE RAIL HEAD (ask 4)

Five-eighths of an inch below the top of the rail head.

  = 5/8 in = 0.625 in = 15.875 mm (exact conversion, 1 in = 25.4 mm)

That is the elevation of the horizontal measurement plane in which the transverse distance is taken. The plane is referenced downward from the top of the rail head (the running surface); the regulation does not vary this depth by rail section, rail weight, or track class — it is a single uniform figure for all track governed by Part 213.

3. CONTEXT — THE LIMITS APPLIED AT THAT PLANE (§ 213.53(b))

The 5/8 in plane is where the following gage WIDTH limits are evaluated (widths, not depths; reproduced so the two numbers are not confused):

  Excepted track:     no minimum,     max 4 ft 10 1/4 in
  Class 1 track:      min 4 ft 8 in,  max 4 ft 10 in
  Class 2 and 3:      min 4 ft 8 in,  max 4 ft 9 3/4 in
  Class 4 and 5:      min 4 ft 8 in,  max 4 ft 9 1/2 in

Nominal U.S. standard gauge is 4 ft 8 1/2 in = 56.5 in = 1435 mm (a width). The 5/8 in (0.625 in) figure above is the depth of the measurement plane and is unrelated to these widths.

4. CORROBORATION WITHIN PART 213

The same five-eighths-of-an-inch reference elevation is used elsewhere in Part 213 for geometry referenced to the rail head, which confirms it is the agency's standard gage-point elevation:
  - § 213.55, footnote 1: alinement line endpoints "at points on the gage side of the line rail, five-eighths of an inch below the top of the railhead."
  - § 213.55, footnotes 2 and (b) footnote 1: chord endpoints "on the gage side of the outer rail, five-eighths of an inch below the top of the railhead."
  - § 213.143, footnote 2 (frog guard rails and guard faces): "A line five-eighths of an inch below the top of the center line of the head of the running rail ..."

5. VERSION / EFFECTIVE-DATE VERIFICATION (ask 2)

The answer is stated for the text in force on 2026-11-21. Verification trail:
  - eCFR, 49 CFR 213.53 (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-II/part-213/subpart-C/section-213.53), fetched 2026-11-23T11:49:21Z, sha256 c2bbfde68769 — a capture two days AFTER the question's date; § 213.53(a) reads exactly as quoted above.
  - eCFR Subpart C page (same fetch session, sha256 88c19123a492) — identical § 213.53(a) text.
  - GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 49 vol. 4, § 213.53 (2025-10-01 edition, sha256 257a5a2da36c) — identical text.
  - GovInfo, CFR 2024 title 49 vol. 4, part 213 (sha256 2f72f0e89052) — identical text.
  - GovInfo, CFR 2016 title 49 vol. 4, part 213 (sha256 6820359ac4ee) — identical text.
  Consequently the five-eighths-of-an-inch figure has been unchanged across the 2016, 2024 and 2025 print editions and the current eCFR text captured after 2026-11-21; nothing in the amendment history of § 213.53 alters it. (The April 28, 2026 amendment visible in Subpart C — 91 FR 22735 — attaches to § 213.63 track-surface/crosslevel provisions, not to § 213.53(a).)

6. FIELD / PRACTICE NOTES (not part of the regulatory answer)

  - A track gage (manual or TGMS) contacts the rail heads on their gage faces with the contact points set 5/8 in below the top of rail; readings taken at other elevations are not Part 213 gage.
  - On track with crosslevel (one rail higher than the other), the plane is taken as the plane through the two rail-head tops, i.e., the 5/8 in offset is applied downward from the top of rail on each rail; the regulation does not separately address the tilted-plane case.
  - Rail-head wear, shelling or mismatch can move the effective contact surface; measurement is referenced to the actual top of the rail head as found, per the regulatory wording.
  - § 213.14 (application of requirements to curved track) and § 213.13 (measuring track not under load) govern how the § 213.53 limits are applied; neither changes the 5/8 in measurement elevation.

BOTTOM LINE
  Where: between the heads of the rails (gage-side faces of the two rail heads), at right angles to the rails.
  How far below the top of rail head: five-eighths of an inch (5/8 in = 0.625 in = 15.875 mm).
  Authority: 49 CFR § 213.53(a), text unchanged and verified in force as of 2026-11-21.
